title: $250M Apple AI Settlement – iPhone 15/16 Users Can Claim $25 to $95 per Device
content:
$250M Apple Intelligence Siri Settlement — iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 Buyers Can Claim $25 to $95 per Device
PublishedSeptember 21, 2026
U.S. residents who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or any iPhone 16 model in the United States between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025 may qualify to claim $25 per device, adjustable up to $95, from the Apple Intelligence Siri false advertising class action settlement. Claims close December 21, 2026.
Claims are open. The claim period began September 21, 2026, and every claim must be submitted
online or postmarked by December 21, 2026. That is also the last day to opt out of or
object to the settlement. Judge Noël Wise of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District
of California granted preliminary approval on July 17, 2026; the final approval hearing is set
for February 24, 2027 at 9:00 a.m. in San Jose, and no payment can be sent before the court
rules and any appeals are resolved. No payment date has been announced. Apple denies every
allegation in the lawsuit and the settlement is not an admission of wrongdoing.

StatusClaims Open
Claim DeadlineDecember 21, 2026Submitted online or postmarked · also the opt-out and objection deadline
Estimated Payout$25 per eligible iPhoneAdjusted pro rata · up to $95 per device if few claims are filed, less than $25 if many are
Proof RequiredNoNo receipt and no Claim ID needed to file online · enter the iPhone serial number, or the Apple Account email and phone number for the device
What Changed Recently?
The notice program and the claim period opened on September 21, 2026, two months after the court
granted preliminary approval on July 17, 2026. Until then there was nothing for an iPhone owner to
do: plaintiffs filed their motion for preliminary approval on May 5, 2026, the court heard it on
June 17, and the settlement website sat on a coming-soon page for the rest of the summer. The
online claim form, the paper claim forms for individuals and for businesses, and the long-form
notice are now live at the official settlement website, Smartphone AI Settlement.
The case itself dates to the iPhone 16 launch. At its developer conference on June 10, 2024, Apple
introduced Apple Intelligence and a redesigned Siri that it said would understand a user's personal
context, act across apps and respond to what was on screen. The lawsuit, Landsheft v. Apple
Inc., alleges that Apple marketed those Siri features as capabilities of the iPhone 16 lineup
and of the iPhone 15 Pro models that ran Apple Intelligence, when the features did not ship with
the phones and were later delayed. Plaintiffs brought claims under consumer protection laws in
several states. The class period ends on March 29, 2025, around the time Apple publicly
acknowledged that the personalized Siri features would take longer than planned.
Apple denies all of the allegations, denies that it did anything improper or unlawful, and has
asserted defenses to every claim. The court has not decided who is right. Both sides agreed to
settle to avoid the cost and risk of a trial, and the notice says in as many words that the
settlement is not an admission of guilt or wrongdoing of any kind.
Who Qualifies?
You are a Settlement Class Member if you reside in the United States and purchased one of seven
iPhone models in the United States between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025 for purposes
other than resale. The settlement website adds that you must be the original purchaser of the
device. Individuals and businesses both qualify; the claim form for a business is filed by an
authorized representative who works for the entity and knows about the purchases.
To be paid you also confirm on the claim form that, when you bought the phone, you expected to
receive certain Siri Apple Intelligence features and did not receive them. That certification is
the substance of the claim, and the form is signed under a declaration that the information is
true and correct and may be audited.
Excluded from the class are Apple, any company Apple controls, Apple's directors, officers and
employees, its legal representatives, successors and assigns, and the judicial officers assigned to
the case along with their staff and immediate families. Anyone who bought a covered phone to resell
it is outside the class, as is anyone who bought a used or refurbished unit from someone other than
the original seller.
The seven eligible iPhone models
The class turns on the model, not on the storage size, the color, the carrier or where you bought
it. An eligible iPhone from an Apple Store, a carrier store, Best Buy, Amazon, Costco or a
carrier's website all counts the same. The model name appears under Settings, General, About on
the phone itself.
The standard iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus are not eligible devices because they never ran Apple
Intelligence. The iPhone 14 and every earlier model are out for the same reason. The iPhone 17
line is out because it launched after the class period closed. An iPhone 15 Pro bought at launch
in September 2023 does not qualify either; the purchase has to fall on or after June 10, 2024, the
day Apple announced the features at issue.
How Much Can You Get?
The notice sets the payment at $25 per Eligible Device. That figure is a starting point, not
a guarantee: it can be increased pro rata, up to a maximum of $95 per device, or decreased pro rata,
depending on the total number of valid claims and devices claimed and on what the court awards in
attorneys' fees, litigation expenses, service awards and notice and administration costs. All of
those come out of the $250 million Total Settlement Amount before class members are paid.
The direction of the adjustment depends on the claim rate. Plaintiffs' preliminary approval papers
estimated that tens of millions of iPhones fall inside the class definition, which is why the $25
figure can move in either direction: a low claim rate leaves more of the fund per device, up to the
$95 ceiling, and a claim rate higher than the parties assumed pushes the per-device amount below
$25. Neither outcome is knowable until the December 21, 2026 deadline passes and the administrator
finishes validating claims. Treat every per-device figure on this page as an estimate.
Each Eligible Device is a separate claim. An individual who bought two covered iPhones in the class
period submits two claim forms, one per serial number, and is paid for each. A business that bought
a fleet of eligible phones files once and attaches a list of the devices. The class
representatives may ask for service awards of up to $2,000 each, and Class Counsel will file a
motion for attorneys' fees and expenses that the settlement website is required to post by
November 17, 2026, five weeks before the claim deadline, so class members can read it before
deciding whether to object. How a
pro rata distribution
works in general is covered in our glossary.
What Proof or Notice ID Is Required?
No receipt, order confirmation or notice is required. When you start a claim on the settlement
website, the first screen asks whether you have a Claim ID and PIN. Class members Apple's records
identified received one by email or postcard, and entering it pre-fills the form. Everyone else
picks the option for filing without a Claim ID and PIN and goes on to the same claim form, so a
buyer who never received a notice is not locked out.
What the form does require is information that identifies the phone. The primary field is the
iPhone serial number, which is under Settings, General, About on the device, printed on the
barcode label of the original box, and usually on the receipt or invoice. If you no longer have the
serial number, the form lets you check a box and instead provide the Apple Account email address
(the Apple Account ID) and the phone number

report.summary: Apple's $250M settlement lets iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 buyers claim $25–$95 per device over allegedly false Apple Intelligence Siri advertising.
report.background: At WWDC on June 10, 2024, Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence and a rebuilt Siri that would understand personal context, act across apps and read on-screen content — features it tied to the iPhone 16 lineup and iPhone 15 Pro. Those personalized Siri capabilities did not ship on launch and slipped well past Apple's advertised window; Apple publicly acknowledged the delay around March 2025. The resulting suit, Landsheft v. Apple Inc., alleged violations of several states' consumer protection laws over marketing that promised unreleased functionality. The case fits a broader pattern of AI hype meeting legal reality: vendors rush to attach 'AI' promises to hardware launches, then miss deadlines while regulators and buyers grow less tolerant of capability claims that amount to roadmaps. Apple denies wrongdoing, and the settlement is not an admission of liability.
key_points: Who qualifies: U.S. residents who were the original purchasers of an iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max or any iPhone 16 model bought between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025 for personal or business use, not resale. Storage, color, carrier and retailer are irrelevant, but a 15 Pro bought at its September 2023 launch does not qualify.

What you can get: a base of $25 per eligible device, adjusted pro rata up to $95 if few claims are filed, or below $25 if the claim rate runs high. Each device is a separate claim, so two phones mean two forms; businesses file once with a device list.

How to file: claims opened September 21, 2026 and must be submitted online or postmarked by December 21, 2026 — a date that doubles as the opt-out and objection deadline. No receipt is required; you identify the phone by serial number, or by the Apple Account email and phone number.

Where the case stands: Judge Noël Wise granted preliminary approval on July 17, 2026, with a final approval hearing set for February 24, 2027 in San Jose. No payments can be issued before that ruling and any appeals are resolved, so no payout date exists yet.

The money math: the $250 million fund first covers attorneys' fees, litigation expenses, service awards of up to $2,000 per class representative, and notice and administration costs. Plaintiffs' filings estimated tens of millions of eligible iPhones, which is why the per-device figure is genuinely uncertain until claims are validated.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the settlement is a pricing signal on overpromising: marketing unreleased model capabilities to sell hardware now carries measurable financial risk, even without an admission of fault. Expect legal teams to scrub 'coming soon' AI feature claims, hedge launch language and coordinate disclosures with actual ship dates. For developers, it is a reminder that platform roadmaps are not contracts — plan integrations around shipped APIs, not keynotes. Apple's Foundation Models framework and rebuilt Siri remain the real targets for anyone building on-device AI. For regular users, it is mostly a low-effort payout with a hard December 21, 2026 deadline, plus a durable lesson: treat AI launch demos as intent, not deliverables, and keep receipts and serial numbers.
report.tools: To follow the case, watch the official settlement site plus class action trackers such as OpenClassActions, Top Class Actions and the FTC's consumer alerts. For broader context on buildable on-device AI, look at Apple's Foundation Models framework documentation, MLX and llama.cpp for local model experiments, and Open Interpreter or Home Assistant's Assist for open assistants that ship the cross-app behavior Siri was criticized for lacking.
